title: The Lamb's People and Two Harvests
overview: After the beasts of chapter 13, John sees the Lamb's faithful people safe with him, hears three angels bring good news, a fallen Babylon and a fearful warning, and then watches the earth being harvested like grain and grapes.

parts.label: The Lamb on Mount Zion (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The Lamb, Revelation's picture of Jesus, stands on Zion, Jerusalem's holy hill, with 144,000 people who carry God's name on their foreheads instead of the beast's mark from chapter 13. Many read the number (12 times 12 times 1,000) as all of God's people, while others see Jewish believers in particular, and only these rescued people can learn their new song.

parts.label: Who the 144,000 are (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Calling them virgins who kept themselves from women pictures them as men, which many readers find jarring. Most take it as faithfulness to God, since the Hebrew Scriptures call idol worship adultery, though some think of soldiers kept pure for holy war or of literal celibacy; as firstfruits, the first part of a harvest given to God, they hint that more will follow.

parts.label: Good news, fallen city (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: An angel brings good news that lasts forever to every nation, calling people to honour God the Creator because the hour of judgment has come, almost like a last appeal. A second angel echoes Isaiah's cry that Babylon has fallen; many scholars think Babylon stands for Rome, the empire of John's day, which made the nations drunk on its unfaithfulness, while others see any proud power set against God.

parts.label: Warning, endurance and rest (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: A third angel warns that those who worship the beast will drink God's anger at full strength, like wine not watered down as was usual, tormented with burning sulfur before the angels and the Lamb while smoke rises forever, images borrowed from the fates of Sodom and Edom. Christians differ on whether this means endless conscious punishment (the traditional view) or final destruction, and the section then calls God's people to endure and promises rest to those who die faithful.

parts.label: The grain harvest (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: One like a son of man, a title from Daniel 7 that Christians read as Jesus, sits crowned on a white cloud and reaps the earth once an angel from the temple says the harvest is ripe. Some take this as the gathering in of God's people and others as judgment, because the text does not say which.

parts.label: The grape harvest (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: Another angel gathers the earth's grapes and throws them into God's great winepress of anger, a judgment image drawn from Isaiah 63 and Joel 3, and blood flows as high as horses' bridles for 1,600 stadia (furlongs in older translations), about 300 kilometres. It is a deliberately horrifying picture of slaughter; many read the numbers as symbolic (1,600 is 4 times 4 times 100, perhaps meaning the whole land or world), and the city is not named, though many think of Jerusalem.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether this chapter describes events still to come at the end of history, the struggle with Rome in John's own day, a sweep of later church history, or timeless patterns of faithfulness and judgment that repeat in every age.
think: This chapter pictures a few people refusing to bow to a power nearly everyone else serves; is there anything you would refuse to go along with even if it cost you a great deal?
